stops.name: Sucre, the Coripata tambo, the box with the sabre
stops.campa: In her last years Juana lives in a whitewashed room off a travelers' inn in the Coripata quarter of Sucre, walls of adobe, beams gnawed by rats, a bed of native cane matting. The historian Gabriel René Moreno and others who seek her out find an old woman who says little and keeps, within reach, a small wooden box holding Belgrano's sabre, her commission as teniente coronel, and her medals, the whole of her rank reduced to what fits in a single chest. To those who ask how she bears it she is remembered saying only that the one thing left to leave her daughter is her tears.
stops.quote: The only thing I can leave my daughter are my tears.
stops.quote_source: Popular tradition, widely cited in Argentine and Bolivian biographical accounts of her final years

stops.name: Sucre, death in the common grave
stops.campa: Juana dies on 25 May 1862, eighty-one years old, in the small rented room where Indalecio Sandi has kept her company on a cot of his own. Sandi carries word to the military authorities and asks for the funeral honors due a coronel of the republic; Major Joaquín Taborga turns him away, the garrison being occupied that day with the festivities of Independence Day, the anniversary of the revolution she helped begin at Chuquisaca fifty-three years before. She is buried in the town cemetery in a common grave, a priest's brief prayer the whole of the ceremony, the cost of the burial one peso.
